paras.text: Business Management, Estimating, Finance, Personnel and Workers Comp, Audio Lecture

This is the biggest block on the business and law half of your exam. Out of fifty business and law questions, roughly nineteen come from this one chapter. Six on project management and administration, six on accounting and finance, four on types of business organization, two on personnel, and one on estimating.
Nineteen out of fifty. More than a third of that section lives here. If you learn nothing else properly, learn this chapter properly.

It is also the chapter with actual arithmetic in it, and I am going to slow all the way down on the one calculation I can nearly promise you will see, which is markup versus margin. Everything else here is comparison. Two things that look alike, and knowing which is which.
Idea one. The five business structures, compared on two axes.
Only two questions matter for each structure. Who can they come after if things go wrong, and how is it taxed.

A sole proprietorship needs no state filing at all. It is the simplest thing there is, and the price of that simplicity is unlimited personal liability. The house, the truck, the savings account, all exposed. All profit lands on your personal return and every dollar gets hit with self employment tax.

A general partnership is the same idea with two or more people, and it is worse than most people realize. Each partner has unlimited joint and several liability. That phrase means a creditor can collect the entire partnership debt from any one partner, including a debt the other partner ran up without you. One bad partner can take your house.

The L L C fixes the liability problem. You file Articles of Organization with LARA, and as long as you maintain the veil, your personal assets are protected. Maintaining the veil means separate bank accounts, no commingling of money, adequate capitalization, and contracts signed in the company name. Taxes pass through to you by default.

Then the S corporation, and here is the trap the exam builds on it. S corp status is not a Michigan filing. It is a federal election you make with the I R S on form twenty five fifty three. You do not go to LARA to become an S corp. It gives you pass through taxation, but an owner who works in the business must take a reasonable W two salary.
And the C corporation, which is the double taxation entity. The corporation pays tax on its profits, then the shareholders pay tax again on the dividends. Small builders almost never want it.

One housekeeping number that gets tested. The L L C annual statement is due to LARA by February fifteenth every year, and the fee is twenty five dollars. Miss it for about two years and the company falls to not in good standing status. But note the distinction, that status is restorable. The company does not automatically dissolve.
Question. Which structure is created by a federal election rather than a Michigan filing, and what date does an L L C owe its annual statement.
The S corporation, by election with the I R S on form twenty five fifty three. And February fifteenth, twenty five dollars.
Idea two. Cash versus accrual, and the two financial statements.

Cash basis records income when the money actually arrives and expenses when they are actually paid. Accrual records income when it is earned, meaning when you bill it, and expenses when they are incurred.
For real job costing you need accrual, because it matches the revenue to the cost that produced it. Cash basis will tell you that you had a great March because a February job finally paid.
For long term contracts, know the two revenue methods by name. Percentage of completion recognizes revenue as the work progresses. Completed contract recognizes it all at the end.
Now the two statements, and the difference is time.
The balance sheet is a snapshot at a single point in time. It is built on the accounting equation, assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity. Always, in every question, no exceptions.
The income statement, the profit and loss, covers a period of time. Revenue minus direct job costs gives gross profit. Gross profit minus overhead gives net profit.
So if a question asks where the year's profit shows up, the answer is the income statement, not the balance sheet. Snapshot versus period. That is the whole distinction.
Idea three. Markup versus margin, which is the calculation on this exam.
Stay with me here, because this is the one people get wrong in business as well as on the test.
Markup is a percentage of your cost. Margin is a percentage of the selling price. They are never the same number, and margin is always the smaller of the two.
Work it with me. A job costs one hundred thousand dollars. You add a twenty five percent markup, so you sell it for one hundred twenty five thousand. Your profit is twenty five thousand dollars.
Now ask the margin question. Twenty five thousand of profit out of the one hundred twenty five thousand you sold it for. That is twenty percent.
Same job, same money, two different numbers. A twenty five percent markup is a twenty percent margin.

Now the famous ten and ten. Ten percent overhead plus ten percent profit is a twenty percent markup, and it produces a margin of only sixteen point six seven percent. That gap is where contractors quietly go broke, thinking they made twenty and actually making sixteen and a half.
Two formulas to carry. Margin equals markup divided by one plus markup. And to hit a target margin, divide your cost by one minus the margin.

Watch the second one, because the trap is built right into it. To earn a twenty percent margin on an eighty thousand dollar job, you divide eighty thousand by point eight, which prices it at one hundred thousand. If you instead multiply by one point two you get ninety six thousand, and you just fell into the trap. Divide by one minus the margin. Do not multiply.
Question. Job costs sixty thousand. You want a twenty five percent margin. What is the price.

Sixty thousand divided by point seven five, which is eighty thousand dollars. If you multiplied by one point two five you got seventy five thousand, which is a twenty five percent markup and only a twenty percent margin.
Idea four. Two more money formulas, then cash flow.
Overhead rate is total annual overhead divided by total annual direct costs. One hundred twenty six thousand of overhead against eight hundred forty thousand of direct cost is fifteen percent.

Break even revenue is fixed overhead divided by gross margin percentage. One hundred fifty thousand of overhead at a thirty percent margin means you need five hundred thousand dollars of revenue just to get to zero.
Now cash flow, and this is the part that kills real companies. Contractors pay for labor and materials before the owner pays them. That timing gap is the business.

Accounts receivable is money owed to you. Accounts payable is money you owe. A company with big receivables and no cash is profitable on paper and dying in real life. That sentence is the answer to more than one exam question and to a lot of contractor bankruptcies.

Underbilling means you have done more work than you have billed, so you are financing the owner's project out of your own pocket. Overbilling is the reverse. Bill promptly and keep your billings matched to the work in place.

Billing runs off a schedule of values, which is the contract price broken into line items. The industry forms are A I A G seven zero two, the payment application summary, and G seven zero three, the line by line continuation sheet. Seven zero two summarizes, seven zero three itemizes.

Retainage is the five to ten percent the owner withholds from each draw until substantial or final completion. Note this for Michigan, there is no statutory cap on retainage for private residential work.

And a lien safe draw schedule ties each draw to a completed milestone, with each check exchanged for a conditional lien waiver. Conditional, because it only takes effect when the payment actually clears. Never sign an unconditional waiver before the money is in your bank, because an unconditional waiver is effective immediately whether you got paid or not.
Idea five. Estimating math, which is free money on this exam.
Board feet. Nominal thickness times nominal width times length in feet, divided by twelve. So a two by six that is ten feet long is two times six times ten over twelve, which is ten board feet.
Concrete. Length times width times thickness, all in feet, gives you cubic feet. Divide by twenty seven for cubic yards, because a cubic yard is three by three by three.

Work one. A four inch slab, twenty four feet by thirty six feet. Four inches is one third of a foot. Twenty four times thirty six times one third is two hundred eighty eight cubic feet. Divide by twenty seven and you get about ten point seven yards. Then you order twelve, because of waste.
A roofing square is one hundred square feet. That one is just memory.
Waste factors. Framing lumber ten to fifteen percent. Drywall ten to twelve. Shingles ten to fifteen. Concrete five to ten. And engineered trusses essentially zero, because they are built to order.

Contingency is a risk reserve, five to ten percent on new construction and ten to twenty percent on remodels. And here is the tested part, contingency goes into the estimate before overhead and profit, because it is not profit. It is money set aside for what you cannot see yet.

Contract types by risk, same idea as the contracts chapter. Lump sum puts the cost risk on you and needs complete plans. Cost plus puts the risk on the owner and fits unknown scope, ideally with a not to exceed cap. Time and materials is hourly plus materials for small or undefined work. Unit price fits work where quantities are uncertain, like excavation.

And an allowance is a plug number for something not yet selected, a tile budget before anyone picked tile. The difference gets settled by written change order. In Michigan, every change order is in writing, and you know why by now, your lien rights depend on it.
Question. Four inch slab, twenty by thirty feet. How many cubic yards, before waste.
Twenty times thirty times one third is two hundred cubic feet. Divided by twenty seven is about seven point four yards.
Idea six. Project management, and the critical path.
The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks through the job, and it sets the minimum project duration. Tasks on the critical path have zero float.

Float, sometimes called slack, is how long a task can slip without moving the completion date. So a task with float can run late and hurt nobody. A task on the critical path runs late and the whole job moves.
That is why the critical path is the longest chain and not the shortest. It is the chain you cannot compress by working around it.
A Gantt chart is the standard bar chart picture of a schedule, but note its limitation, it does not inherently show dependencies. Network diagrams do.

Substantial completion means the owner can use the work for its intended purpose. It triggers the punch list, the warranty clock, and release of most retainage. Final completion means everything is done, punch list included.

And the three bonds, one line each. The bid bond guarantees you honor your bid. The performance bond guarantees you finish the work. The payment bond guarantees your subs and suppliers get paid. When the exam asks which bond protects subcontractors, it is the payment bond, every time.
Idea seven. Employee or independent contractor, and the payroll numbers.

Whether somebody is your employee is decided by the I R S common law test, which looks at behavioral control, financial control, and the relationship of the parties, built on the twenty factors of revenue ruling eighty seven forty one. Michigan's workers comp statute adopted that exact twenty factor test for anything on or after January first, twenty thirteen.
And one shortcut worth remembering. If you withhold federal income tax for somebody, that alone is prima facie evidence they are your employee. You have already treated them like one.
Now the payroll numbers, and they come in pairs.

F I C A is six point two percent social security plus one point four five percent medicare, which is seven point six five percent. The employer pays that, and the employee pays the same. Seven point six five each side.
Federal unemployment, F U T A, is six percent of the first seven thousand dollars of wages, but with the state credit it nets down to point six percent.
Withheld taxes are trust fund taxes. That name matters, because owners are personally liable if they do not get remitted. The corporate veil does not protect you there.

Michigan unemployment through the U I A. The statutory default taxable wage base is nine thousand five hundred dollars, but it drops to nine thousand dollars for qualified employers, meaning those with all reports filed and no unpaid balance, while the trust fund stays healthy. Nine thousand is the base that actually applies in twenty twenty five and twenty twenty six. Know both numbers, because the exam can ask for either.

New employers pay two point seven percent, except construction. A new construction employer pays the average rate for the construction industry, which is several times higher. That exception is exactly the kind of thing this exam loves, so expect to see two point seven offered as a wrong answer for a builder.

One genuine change for twenty twenty six. The ten ninety nine reporting threshold rose from six hundred dollars to two thousand dollars for payments made this year. Older study materials still say six hundred, so trust this over an old book.

Overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act is one and a half times the regular rate for hours over forty in a workweek. And note the negative, there is no federal daily overtime. Twelve hours on Monday is not overtime by itself.

MIOSHA recordkeeping. Employers with eleven or more employees keep the form three hundred injury log, post the annual summary from February first to April thirtieth, and keep the records five years. Report a fatality within eight hours. Report an in patient hospitalization, an amputation, or the loss of an eye within twenty four hours.
Eight hours for a death, twenty four for the other three.
Question. Give me the F I C A rate on each side, and the two MIOSHA reporting clocks.
Seven point six five percent from the employer and seven point six five from the employee. Fatality within eight hours, and hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within twenty four hours.
Idea eight. Michigan workers compensation.

The law is the Workers Disability Compensation Act, and here is a detail people miss, it is administered by the Workers Disability Compensation Agency under the Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity. Not LARA. Different agency from the one that licenses you.
It is a no fault system and it is the exclusive remedy. The injured worker gets benefits, medical, wage loss, vocational rehabilitation, and death benefits, but cannot sue you.
Coverage is required if you hit either of two triggers, and either one alone is enough.
Trigger one, you regularly employ three or more employees at one time, part timers included.
Trigger two, even with fewer than three, if just one employee has worked thirty five or more hours a week for thirteen weeks or longer during the preceding fifty two weeks.
A sole proprietor with no employees is exempt but may opt in.

Owners can be excluded by filing form W C three thirty seven. That covers a corporate officer who owns at least ten percent of a corporation with ten or fewer stockholders, an L L C member manager who owns at least ten percent of an L L C with ten or fewer members, or a partner. Ten percent ownership, ten or fewer owners.

Now the general contractor trap, and you met its cousin in the lien chapter. If your sub has no workers comp and no valid exclusion on file, and his worker gets hurt on your site, the claim lands on you. So you collect the comp certificate or the exclusion form before anybody swings a hammer.

Penalties for going bare are serious. It is a misdemeanor, up to one thousand dollars and up to six months, and every single day is a separate offense. On top of that the state can get a court injunction shutting you down, plus a civil fine of up to one thousand dollars per day, looking back three years.
And the worst part is not the fine. An uninsured employer loses the exclusive remedy shield, which means the injured worker can sue you in civil court, with no cap.
One last insurance term. The experience modification rate, the E M R. One point zero is average. Below one means a good safety record and cheaper premiums, above one means the opposite.
Question. You have two employees. One of them works forty hours a week and has for the last six months. Do you need workers comp coverage.

Yes. You fail trigger one with only two employees, but trigger two catches you, one employee at thirty five or more hours a week for thirteen weeks or more in the preceding fifty two. Either trigger alone requires coverage.

One more number before the recap, because it shows up and it is easy. Michigan sales tax is six percent. The contractor pays it on materials. Labor is exempt, and you never charge sales tax on the contract price.
Rapid fire recap. Say these with me.

Michigan sales tax, six percent, contractor pays on materials, labor exempt, never charged on the contract price. L L C annual statement, February fifteenth, twenty five dollars. Markup to margin, twenty percent markup is sixteen point seven margin, twenty five markup is twenty margin, fifty markup is thirty three point three margin. Board feet, thickness times width times length over twelve. Concrete, cubic feet divided by twenty seven. Roofing square, one hundred square feet. Contingency, five to ten new, ten to twenty remodel, and it goes in before profit. Retainage, five to ten percent. Workers comp triggers, three employees at one time, or one employee at thirty five hours for thirteen weeks in the last fifty two. Exclusion, form W C three thirty seven, ten or fewer owners, ten percent or more ownership. Penalty, a thousand dollars, six months, each day separate, plus a thousand a day civil. Independent contractor test, I R S twenty factors, adopted in Michigan since January first twenty thirteen. F I C A, seven point six five each side. F U T A, point six percent net on the first seven thousand. U I A wage base, nine thousand five hundred statutory default, nine thousand for qualified employers right now. New construction employers pay the industry average, not two point seven. Ten ninety nine threshold, two thousand dollars starting this year. Overtime, time and a half over forty per week, no federal daily overtime. MIOSHA, three hundred log at eleven employees, fatality in eight hours, hospitalization, amputation, or eye in twenty four. Payment bond pays the subs. Conditional waiver until the check clears. Assets equal liabilities plus equity.

That is nineteen questions worth of material. The two things to drill tonight are the markup and margin arithmetic, because it is the only real math in the section, and the workers comp triggers, because they show up in two different chapters. Run the deck until the numbers come without thinking.
